title: Newborns looked longer at upright faces only with dark features on a light ground
summary: Farroni and colleagues found that newborns looked longer at an upright face-like image than an inverted one only when the eye and mouth areas were darker than the surrounding face.
body: In their 2005 PNAS paper, Farroni and colleagues tested 105 newborns, 13 to 168 hours old, at two hospitals in Italy. When a schematic head had dark squares where eyes and a mouth would be, on a lighter head, the babies looked longer at the upright pattern than at the upside-down one. When the contrast was reversed, that upright advantage was not found. Photographs of a woman's face showed the same kind of gap: a strong upright preference in ordinary contrast, and no significant upright preference when the contrast was flipped. The authors say the result fits either sensitivity to shadowed areas under overhead light or a bias toward patterns that could be eye contact, and they do not decide between those two readings. The result is about babies in the first week. It is not a claim about older infants.

sources.title: Newborns' preference for face-relevant stimuli: Effects of contrast polarity
sources.author: Teresa Farroni, Mark H. Johnson, Enrica Menon, Luisa Zulian, Dino Faraguna, and Gergely Csibra
sources.note: Supports Experiment 1a and Experiment 2a: upright preference under positive contrast polarity, and its absence under reversed polarity, plus the authors' two unread-as-decided functional accounts. Paraphrase of the opened PMC full text. A copyright line granting CC BY was not on the page, so no sentence is quoted.
